gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the one instrument-measured three-added-screen extender under $600 (ServeTheHome on the $479 KYY X90G: 284.6 at the 100% setting, 83% sRGB, 1010:1) fell short of its maker's 400-nit rating, or that none of ChatGPT's picks (Trio 3 Pro, UPERFECT BE14BF, INVZI MagHub Dual 14) has a named-lab panel measurement behind it.
standout_why: Compared against the two cited pages and four other results. uperfect.com's roundup (cited) gives only maker specs ("up to 300 nits", "100% sRGB") with no tester named. mobilepixels.us/products/trio (cited) returned HTTP 429, so I could not read it. theofficejournal.com (rank 1) has no measured figure. PCWorld's KYY review (in the results, uncited) already has the weighed 6.5 lb against the 3.5 lb claim and the 15%-in-33-minutes battery drain, so the weight finding is not new. TechRadar's KYY X90E review (in the results) already shows "82% sRGB". Our own /best-triple-laptop-screen-extender already carries Macworld's brightness-on-laptop-power note and CHIP.pl's 11 W for the Trio 3 Pro. What is new is ServeTheHome's brightness, contrast and sRGB table for the X90G and Notebookcheck's FOPO 12-inch panel figures, but neither covers a product we would pick.
decides: It does not change the pick; it adds a caveat. No named lab has measured the Trio 3 Pro's panels: Macworld and CHIP.pl only report that it cannot reach its 300-nit maximum on laptop power, and CHIP lists 11 W in use. So the Trio 3 Pro stays a pick on resolution and video path, not on measured brightness. For shoppers who want three added screens under $600, the measured rival (KYY X90G) came in below its brightness claim and weighed nearly double its claimed weight; there is no measurement of the FOPO S788 to set against that, so the page should not claim the S788 is brighter or lighter in practice.
